primitives.name: Interval-Score ROC Curve
primitives.verbatim_quote: - **IS–ROC curve:** β ↦ (MS^P(β), MAD^P(β)) — mean interval width vs.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'β': 'coverage level, dimensionless in (0,1]', 'MS^P(β)': 'mean interval width, same units as X', 'MAD^P(β)': 'mean absolute deviation, same units as X'}
primitives.assumptions: Forecasting distributions are indexed by coverage β, with nested intervals satisfying l_β ≤ q_{β/2} ≤ q_{1-β/2} ≤ u_β.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At β=1, intervals collapse to point forecasts; at β→0, intervals become infinitely wide.

layer2.mapping: The IS–ROC curve maps predictive performance across coverage levels, enabling comparison of forecasters' trade-offs between sharpness and accuracy in a geometric space.
layer2.telemetry: Per-coverage dominance regions and Pareto-optimal frontiers.

primitives.name: Tunable Interval Predictor
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model - **Tunable Interval Predictor (TIP):** P(β,x)=[l_β(x),u_β(x)] with nesting property and merging at β=1 (point forecast); every predictive distribution induces a TIP via central intervals l_β=q_{β/2}, u_β=q_{1-β/2}.
primitives.latex: P(\beta, x) = [l_\beta(x), u_\beta(x)] \quad \text{where } l_\beta = q_{\beta/2}, u_\beta = q_{1-\beta/2}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'P(β,x)': 'predictive interval, same units as X', 'l_β': 'lower quantile, same units as X', 'u_β': 'upper quantile, same units as X', 'q_γ': 'quantile function, same units as X'}
primitives.assumptions: Predictive distributions admit quantile functions; intervals are nested and merge at β=1.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When β=1, l_β = u_β = q_{1/2} (median); when β→0, l_β → -∞, u_β → +∞.

layer2.mapping: A TIP is a parameterized family of intervals that induces an IS–ROC curve; it provides a bridge between probabilistic forecasts and geometric diagnostics.
layer2.telemetry: Quantile-based interval generation and nesting consistency.

primitives.name: Convex Hull Ensembling
primitives.verbatim_quote: - **Ensembling:** global convex hull over the (convexified) curves of competing TIPs — per α pick the TIP minimizing IS(α,g(α)); isotonic regression restores nesting.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'α': 'target coverage level, dimensionless', 'g(α)': 're-calibrated coverage, dimensionless', 'IS(α, g(α))': 'interval score, same units as X'}
primitives.assumptions: Competing TIPs induce convex IS–ROC curves; isotonic regression ensures nesting after ensembling.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Non-convexity leads to undefined calibration; randomized interpolation required for convex hull segments.

layer2.mapping: The convex hull operation aggregates multiple TIPs into a single optimal predictor by selecting the best-performing forecaster at each coverage level.
layer2.telemetry: Ensemble performance improvement over individual forecasters and coverage-specific optimality.

The IS–ROC curve is defined as a parametric map β ↦ (MS^P(β), MAD^P(β)), where MS^P(β) is the mean interval width and MAD^P(β) is the mean absolute deviation at coverage β. It is derived from a TIP which generates nested intervals via quantiles l_β = q_{β/2}, u_β = q_{1-β/2}. The curve is shown to be convex under general conditions, implying that any convex combination of forecasters lies within the convex hull of their respective IS–ROC curves. This allows for principled ensembling by selecting the TIP that minimizes the interval score at each target coverage α. Tangent calibration aligns forecasters’ slopes with idealized iso-score lines, while step calibration corrects for deviations in non-convex segments. The curve reveals dominance regimes not visible in scalar metrics such as CRPS or MAE. Its geometric structure enables GSE to dynamically adjust its forecasting strategy based on risk tolerance and coverage requirements.
